mini_reading.title: The Ridge Beyond the Marked Trail
mini_reading.passage: On the third morning of school camp, the Year 6 group left the painted markers and climbed toward a ridge the map showed only as a pale smudge. They had been told to notice the weather, the rock, and the way a person speaks when the path grows steep. A thin wind moved through the gums. Nobody treated the walk as a race. Ms Hart asked them to investigate the slope before anyone crossed the loose stone. A patient method mattered more than speed. Oliver paused and tried to determine which trees still held last night's rain, then compare the wet bark with the dry dust. The group had to evaluate whether the safer line was longer but sound, or shorter and likely to crumble. The crumbling edge was one consequence they could not ignore. They did not need a heroic tale. They needed to analyse what they had seen so the next pair would not slip. The change underfoot was significant enough to slow the line. By the fire trail, the better prize was this: they could describe the ridge without exaggeration.

reading_questions.prompt: Which detail is actually in the passage?
options: A visiting reporter took over and published the answer that morning.
The teacher announced a prize for the fastest finished page.
The Year 6 group left the painted markers and climbed toward a ridge.
The class cancelled the activity and went home before anything was recorded.
reading_questions.answer: The Year 6 group left the painted markers and climbed toward a ridge.

reading_questions.prompt: In this passage, "analyse" is used to mean:
options: To work out or decide something after thinking or checking carefully.
To look closely at something so you can understand how it works or what it means.
Important enough to notice or to make a real difference.
The natural world around us, or the conditions in which people or animals live.
reading_questions.answer: To look closely at something so you can understand how it works or what it means.

reading_questions.prompt: Which sentence best states the main idea of the whole passage?
options: The camp walk rewards careful observation and a safe plan more than a dramatic view.
The walk is treated as a race to the ridge and back.
The students ignore the loose stone and take every shortcut.
The camp journal wants a heroic tale more than an accurate description.
reading_questions.answer: The camp walk rewards careful observation and a safe plan more than a dramatic view.

reading_questions.prompt: What can the reader reasonably infer from the passage?
options: He wants the quickest possible conclusion, even without support.
He has already decided that nothing in the scene is worth noticing.
He is only interested in winning a public prize.
The students are expected to notice conditions, not just reach the top.
reading_questions.answer: The students are expected to notice conditions, not just reach the top.

reading_questions.prompt: Which cause-and-effect relationship is supported by the passage?
options: The activity was cancelled, so no notes were kept.
A film version of the event replaced what actually happened.
The slope had loose stone and a crumbling edge. This led to: The group slowed and had to judge which line was safer.
A prize was offered, so everyone rushed and ignored the facts.
reading_questions.answer: The slope had loose stone and a crumbling edge. This led to: The group slowed and had to judge which line was safer.
